title: Media framing of spiders may exacerbate arachnophobic sentiments
screen_reason: Content analysis of 314 spider-related news reports in Italian online newspapers (2010 – February 2020) in which arachnologist authors scored every article for the presence of four types of factual error. 73% contained one or more errors — a share of items in a defined sample judged inaccurate against expert subject knowledge, which the paper itself describes as spreading misinformation. Eligible as CONTENT, though see the borderline flag.

estimates.platform: Italian online newspapers (retrieved via Google News)
estimates.date: Media reports published 2010 to February 2020; retrieval and Facebook-share extraction March 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of Italian online spider-related news reports containing at least one scientific error
estimates.value_raw: One or more error types were present in 73% of media reports (the Abstract states 70% and the Discussion 'Over 70%')
estimates.denominator: 314 media reports on human–spider encounters in Italy published in Italian online newspapers between 2010 and February 2020, retrieved by 260 Google News keyword searches (2 action words x 13 species names x 10 years)
estimates.definition: Presence of at least one of four expert-scored error types: errors in photographs (pictured species does not match the species named, or is unidentifiable); errors in systematics and taxonomy (e.g. calling a spider an 'insect'); errors in venom, physiology or medical terminology; errors in morphology and anatomy (e.g. a spider 'sting' rather than a bite)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Providing the photo of a wrong species, calling a spider 'insect' or stating that a spider 'stings' rather than 'bites', are small errors that contribute to spread misinformation"
estimates.source_quote: One or more error types were present in 73% of media reports (Figure 3).
estimates.page_loc: Results section 3.2 'Quality of media reports', p. 1150; Figure 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Coded by the authors, who are professional arachnologists (including a museum spider taxonomist and researchers routinely consulted by the Milan anti-poison centre and a Turin hospital for spider identification, ~4.6 requests/month in 2019). Each of four error types scored present/absent, with no counting of repeated errors of the same type. No inter-rater reliability statistic is reported for the error coding; three authors did independently code sensationalism and take the consensus, but no kappa is given.
estimates.moderator_quote: We assessed the quality of each media report by checking for the presence/absence of four types of errors in text and figures: 1. Errors in photographs … 2. Errors in systematics and taxonomy … 3. Errors in venom and other physiological or medical aspects or terminology … and 4. Errors in morphology and anatomy … Each error type was scored as present or absent, thus we did not count cumulative errors of the same type in the same report.
estimates.notes: borderline=true on the CONTENT/QUALITY line. Coded CONTENT because items are judged accurate vs inaccurate against expert subject knowledge (an external ground truth) with explicit error coding, not scored on a DISCERN/GQS-style rubric. But the threshold is low: the single most common error type is morphology/anatomy at 55.3%, which the paper illustrates with the terminological slip 'sting' instead of 'bite'. A report whose substantive claims are all correct can therefore be counted as containing an error, which pulls towards QUALITY. An adjudicator may prefer the venom/medical error rate (15%) as the substantively misinformation-like subset. NUMBER DISCREPANCY: Results say 73%, the Abstract 70% and the Discussion 'over 70%'; 73% is used as the most precise in-text statement. YEAR: content spans 2010 to February 2020 with an exponential increase over the decade, so a single year is a poor summary; 2020 recorded as the collection year. topic=science_other (wildlife/arachnology); health_other is a defensible alternative given that the reports concern bites and envenomation.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) ERROR-TYPE SUBSHARES, not extracted as separate rows (components of the 73% headline, all on the same 314-report denominator): morphology and anatomy 55.3%, species photographs 28.4%, systematics and taxonomy 25.8%, venom/physiological aspects 15%. The venom/medical figure is the strictest and most clearly misinformation-like variant and would be the row to add if an adjudicator wants a narrower definition. (2) SENSATIONALISM, 32% of reports coded overstated/sensationalistic by three-author consensus — deliberately NOT extracted: sensationalism is a tone judgement, not a veracity judgement, and a wholly accurate report can be sensationalistic. (3) 'A conservative estimate would suggest that less than 10% of the bites reported in the media reports analysed here were delivered by the species described in the report' — excluded under R8: it is an inference the authors draw from an external source (Suchard 2011), not a measurement made in this study, and it is a bound rather than a point estimate. (4) The three reported L. rufescens fatalities: the Abstract says 'two out of three casualties … were fake news, while the third was unverifiable' but the Results say all three 'were unverifiable'. Denominator of three events, internally inconsistent, so no row. (5) Other descriptive shares are not veracity measures: 86.6% of reports carried a species photograph, ~10% a photograph of the bite, experts were 'sporadically' mentioned ('in virtually none was an expert consulted'), 39.5% of reports were never shared on Facebook. (6) Facebook shares are modelled (sensationalistic reports shared two to three times more than neutral ones) but no share of exposure attributable to erroneous reports is given, so no EXPOSURE or CONCENTRATION row is derivable.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling frame: 260 Google News keyword searches in Italian (bite/sting x 13 general, Latin and vernacular spider names x years 2010–2020), each followed to the last available results page; reports without a named locality, about events outside Italy, or not reporting a specific human–spider encounter were excluded, yielding 314 reports covering 344 events attributable to 97 unique events (mean 3.52 reports per event, range 1–33). Coding by expert arachnologist authors; four binary error types; sensationalism coded independently by three authors with consensus. No reliability statistics reported. Google News indexing is the implicit selection mechanism, and clustering of reports on a few viral events (33 and 31 reports on two single alleged bites) is handled only in the sharing model via a random effect for event ID. Four Facebook-share outliers (>15,000 shares) were dropped from the sharing analysis. Data deposited on Figshare.
rob.item6_quote: We assessed the quality of each media report by checking for the presence/absence of four types of errors in text and figures: 1. Errors in photographs, when the photograph(s) of the species in the media report (if any) did not correspond to the species mentioned in the text, or when the attribution was not possible (e.g. blurry photographs); 2. Errors in systematics and taxonomy, like the common mistake of considering spiders 'insects' … 3. Errors in venom and other physiological or medical aspects or terminology … and 4. Errors in morphology and anatomy, such as the frequent 'spider sting' instead of 'spider bite'.
rob.item10_quote: One or more error types were present in 73% of media reports (Figure 3). … We collected and analysed 314 media reports published between 2010 and 2020, discussing 344 spider-related events attributable to 97 unique events.
